title: Chrome for nurses on Mac: tabs, shortcuts and charting tips for 2026 with Lazur
metaTitle: Chrome for Nurses on Mac: Tabs, Shortcuts and Charting Tips
description: Chrome for nurses on Mac: set up tabs, reopen closed pages, search open tabs and keep charting safe. Tips that work without Lazur, plus voice help.
intro: Chrome for nurses on Mac is the regular Chrome app, set up so you can move between charting, policies and lab results without losing your place. This page covers the settings, tab habits and shortcuts that save time on a 12-hour shift, plus where Lazur fits in. Every tip here works without Lazur.
tldr: Bookmark your charting tabs at the start of shift, so you can rebuild the set in one step.
Type @tabs in the address bar to find a tab fast. Press ⌘⇧T to reopen one you closed by mistake.
On a shared Mac, do not save passwords in Chrome unless your IT team allows it.
Hold ⌥⌘ to ask Lazur about the screen. Lazur points and explains. It does not click for you.
Check your facility's policy before you show patient details to any AI tool, Lazur included.

blocks.text: Nurses do not get a separate version of Chrome. The Mac app is one program, and every tip here uses the regular version. What changes is the setup. You work in long stretches, with interruptions, and often with patient details on screen. The sources behind this page do not measure which browser nurses use for their EHR, or how they use Chrome on a ward. Treat this page as practical advice, not as research on Chrome.
Where your time goes in Chrome on a shift

Charting takes a large share of the shift. A 2025 JMIR Nursing study used EHR vendor time data for February 2023. It put flowsheet charting at 31.11% of a 12-hour nursing shift. The data came from an academic system with four teaching hospitals in the northeastern US.
Nurses in the same study self-reported that 10% to 50% of their shift goes to documenting in the EHR. That range is wide. Your own number may sit far from either end.
Much of the lost time is switching. You open a record, check an order, jump to a policy and come back. Each switch costs a little time and attention. Chrome habits cut how often you go hunting.

Set up Chrome once before your first shift

Start with sign-in, because it decides where your bookmarks live. Google's help page says that when you sign out of Chrome, 'bookmarks and other info are saved only on your device, not in your Google Account.' A signed-out Chrome keeps your bookmarks on that Mac. A signed-in Chrome can keep them on your other devices too.

Passwords work differently. Chrome saves them through Google Password Manager. An optional passphrase encrypts your synced data, so Google cannot read it. If you turn on sync, set that passphrase and store it somewhere safe. The passphrase is what protects your synced data.
To see where you stand, open Chrome > Settings. Sync and sign-in options are listed there. Check them before your first shift, not during one.

blocks.title: Shared Macs
blocks.text: On a Mac other staff use, do not save passwords in Chrome unless your IT team allows it. Sign out of your Google Account when your shift ends.
Pin and bookmark the tabs you need

Use one tab for each screen you check again and again. One example set is the patient list, the medication record, the unit policy page and the lab results page. Your hospital's systems set the real list, so use your own names here.
Save the set so you can rebuild it at the next shift. Work through these steps once:

items: Put the tabs in the order you use them, left to right.
Open More (⋮) > Bookmarks > Bookmark All Tabs.
Save them into a folder named for your unit, if Chrome offers one.
At the next shift, open the folder and choose Open all.
Check that each page loads and that you are signed in before you chart.

blocks.text: Vertical tabs help when the tab strip gets crowded. Right-click the tab bar and choose Show Tabs Vertically. The tabs then run down the side of the window, one per line. Google's Chrome page lists this option.
If you change the set, bookmark it again into a new folder. That way the old set stays intact while you test the new order.
Compare two screens with split view
Split view puts two tabs side by side in one window. Google's Chrome page lists it as a built-in feature. Use it when you need the medication record and an order open together.
Split view works best on a large screen. In a small window, a form gets cramped and fields can be hard to read. Check that the field you need is fully visible before you type.
Pick the two tabs first, then turn on split view from the tab menu. If you cannot find the option, ask Lazur to walk you through it.
Find a lost tab or reopen a closed page
Find a tab from the address bar. Click it, or press ⌘L. Type @tabs, then press Tab or Space. Add a word or two from the page title. Chrome lists the open tabs that match.
Say the policy page is one of many open tabs. Type @tabs, press Space, then type a word from the policy title. The list narrows to the matching tab, and you pick it from there.
Reopen a page you closed by mistake with ⌘⇧T. Chrome brings back the last closed tab. Press it again to go further back through your recent closures.
Reopening a page may not restore what you were doing. A form may have lost text you never saved. Check the page before you continue, and look for a saved or draft state.
What to do when a form freezes

Freezes happen. In a Toronto acute-care study, nurses in focus groups described slow systems, especially with certain forms. One nurse described freezes of about 10 s while charting. That study had 6 focus-group nurses at a single site, so treat it as a report, not a measure.

items: Wait a few seconds before you click again, so you do not repeat an action.
Look for a saved or draft state before you leave the page.
If your policy allows, copy the text into a notes app that holds no patient identifiers, so it is not lost.
Report the freeze to your informatics or IT team, with the time and the form name.

blocks.text: Restart Chrome last, not first. Quit with ⌘Q, then reopen. Bookmarks survive a restart. Unsaved form text may not.
Dictate notes without typing everything

Long notes take time to type, especially when you are standing at a cart. Lazur can dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Hold fn, speak, then let go. Lazur types the text where your cursor sits.

Check every line before you save it. Dictation can mishear drug names and unit terms. Add those terms to Lazur's personal dictionary once, so they come out right next time. Snippets and clipboard slots help with phrases you repeat.
Dictation does not change your facility's rules on what goes into the record. Follow the same policy you would follow when typing.
Where Lazur fits in Chrome on Mac

Lazur is a voice assistant that lives in the notch of your Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.
Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. You make every click, every entry and every submit. That keeps you in control of the record.
Research jobs run in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, not yours. Lazur returns a summary and a report when the job finishes. Your charting tabs stay where you left them.
Patient information and AI tools on the ward

Read this before you use any AI tool near patient data. Lazur listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models.

Sending data is still sending data. Check your facility's policy before you hold the shortcut with a patient name, a medical record number or a date of birth on screen. If the policy does not mention AI tools, ask your IT or privacy team first.
Use Lazur where patient data is absent, such as policy pages, settings and how-to questions. A question like 'where is Bookmark All Tabs' needs no patient data at all.
Mistakes nurses make in Chrome

items: Leaving a patient record open on a screen that others can read.
Saving passwords on a Mac that other staff use.
Assuming bookmarks follow you to another Mac. A signed-out Chrome keeps them on one device.
Closing a tab with unsaved text, then expecting the text back when you reopen the tab.
Typing a patient's name into the address bar, which can leave it in Chrome's history on that Mac.
Changing Chrome or its updates on a managed Mac without asking IT first.

blocks.text: Check your Chrome version and updates

Open Chrome > About Google Chrome to see the version on your Mac. WhatIsMyBrowser, a third-party tracker, lists the latest stable Chrome for Mac as 156.0.8078.82, released 2026-11-04. Google's own homepage does not list a version number, so check Google's release notes before you quote a build.
On a managed Mac, IT often controls updates. Do not work around that. Ask which version your unit should run. That answer beats any tracker.
A worked example for one shift
Here is one way to set up a shift, from start to finish. Your tabs will differ, but the order holds.

items: At the start, open the patient list, the medication record, the unit policy page and the lab results.
Bookmark all tabs into your unit folder, so the set is there next shift.
Put the medication record and the policy page in split view when you need both.
Mid-shift, a tab closes by accident. Press ⌘⇧T to bring it back.
A new policy question comes up. Type @tabs, then a word from the page title, to find the right tab.
At the end, close the patient tabs and sign out of your Google Account on any shared Mac.

blocks.text: The setup takes a few minutes the first time. After that, each tab is one step away. The hunt gets shorter, and the record stays in front of you.
Why browser tips do not fix a long shift

A Toronto study found navigation was the only usability factor significantly tied to nurses' perceptions of EHR use (beta = 0.38, p < .01). Ease of use and workload were not significant in its survey. It covered one acute-care site, with 133 of 329 eligible nurses responding.

The same focus groups said nurses often stayed past shift end to finish documentation. They linked that to duplicate charting. Chrome cannot fix duplicate charting, but it can cut the time spent hunting for the right screen.

A Finnish survey of 3,610 registered nurses found that 17.70% used a mobile version of their EHR. Those nurses reported higher time pressure. That is an association, not proof that mobile use causes the pressure.
So use Chrome to cut the small losses, like lost tabs and slow hunts. The bigger losses come from workload, and a browser cannot fix that.
Next steps for nurses on Mac

If you want voice help on the ward Mac, start with the free trial. Lazur has a free trial with no credit card, and you can compare plans on the [pricing page](/pricing). Download Lazur for macOS on Apple silicon or Intel from the [download page](/download).

Other pages may help too. The [Chrome page](/apps/chrome) covers asking about any page out loud. The [nurse guide](/for/nurses) covers dictation for notes and handoffs. Shift email has its own habits, so see [Outlook for nurses on Mac](/for/nurses/outlook).

faq.question: Is there a special version of Chrome for nurses on Mac?
faq.answer: No. Chrome for Mac is one app. The settings and tab habits on this page apply to the regular version, and you can set them up before your first shift.

faq.question: How do I reopen a closed tab in Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘⇧T. Chrome reopens the last tab you closed, and pressing it again goes further back. Reopening a page may not bring back text you typed but never saved, so check the form first.

faq.question: How do I find a tab in Chrome without scrolling?
faq.answer: Click the address bar or press ⌘L, type @tabs, then press Tab or Space. Add a word or two from the page title to narrow the list. Chrome shows the open tabs that match.

faq.question: Should I sync Chrome on a hospital Mac?
faq.answer: Usually not, unless your IT team allows it. Google says that when you sign out, bookmarks and other info stay only on that device. Sync copies them to your other devices, so check your policy before you turn it on.

faq.question: Can Lazur click through my EHR for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you. It points at what is on screen, guides you one click at a time, and waits for each click.

faq.question: Is it safe to use Lazur with patient information on screen?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you, and they are not stored. Your facility's policy decides whether that is allowed, so check before you hold the shortcut with patient details visible.

faq.question: How much of a shift do nurses spend charting?
faq.answer: In a 2025 JMIR Nursing study, vendor time data put flowsheet charting at 31.11% of a 12-hour shift at one academic system. Nurses in the study self-reported 10% to 50% of their shift on EHR documentation.

faq.question: What Chrome version should I use on a Mac?
faq.answer: WhatIsMyBrowser lists 156.0.8078.82 as the latest stable Chrome for Mac, released 2026-11-04. Check your own version under Chrome > About Google Chrome, and follow your IT team's guidance on updates.
